items.prompt: State the basis for grouping organisms in biological classification.
items.canonical_answer: Features that the organisms share.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: states that organisms are grouped by the features they share, such as body structure; habitat or colour alone earns no mark.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.
objective_titles: State that organisms can be classified into groups by features that they share

items.prompt: Name the first part of a two-part scientific species name.
items.canonical_answer: The genus.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: names the genus as the first part of the name.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.
objective_titles: Describe the binomial system of naming species as a system in which the scientific name of an organism is made up of two parts showing the genus and species

items.prompt: Outline the hierarchy of classification by naming, in order from the broader group to the narrower group, its three most specific levels.
items.canonical_answer: Family, genus, species.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: family, written in first position as the broadest of the three levels.
1 mark: genus, written in second position.
1 mark: species, written in third position as the narrowest level. Each mark needs the level name in its correct position, so a name in the wrong position earns no mark.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.
objective_titles: Outline the use of a hierarchical classification system for living organisms

items.prompt: Panthera leo (lion) and Panthera tigris (tiger) share a genus. Explain why they are still different species.
items.canonical_answer: A genus is a broader group that can contain several species. A species is identified by the whole two-part name, and the specific names leo and tigris differ, so they are different species.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: gives the reason that a genus is a broader group that can contain more than one species.
1 mark: states that the specific names differ (leo and tigris), and a species is identified by the whole two-part name.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.
objective_titles: Outline the use of a hierarchical classification system for living organisms

items.prompt:
Construct a dichotomous key to identify specimens A to D, using only the observations in this table.
| Specimen | Jointed legs | Leg pairs | Antennae pairs |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| A | absent | 0 | 0 |
| B | present | 3 | 1 |
| C | present | 4 | 0 |
| D | present | 5 | 2 |
items.canonical_answer: One possible key: 1a Jointed legs absent → A; 1b Jointed legs present → 2. 2a Two pairs of antennae → D; 2b Fewer than two pairs of antennae → 3. 3a Three pairs of legs → B; 3b Four pairs of legs → C. Any key that separates all four specimens correctly is credited.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: each step gives two contrasting statements, for example legs present or absent.
1 mark: the statements use only features given in the table.
1 mark: the key leads from the first step to a named endpoint for each of A, B, C and D.
1 mark: each specimen reaches one identification only, because the choices cannot overlap and there is no dead end.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.
objective_titles: Construct and use simple dichotomous keys based on easily identifiable features

items.prompt:
Use this key to name the letter reached by each of four animals. (i) no jointed legs; (ii) jointed legs, no antennae; (iii) jointed legs, one pair of antennae; (iv) jointed legs, two pairs of antennae.
1a Jointed legs absent → A
1b Jointed legs present → go to 2
2a Antennae absent → C
2b Antennae present → go to 3
3a One pair of antennae → B
3b Two pairs of antennae → D
items.canonical_answer: (i) A; (ii) C; (iii) B; (iv) D.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: (i) A, reading jointed legs absent at step 1a, so the key ends there.
1 mark: (ii) C, reading jointed legs present at 1b and antennae absent at 2a.
1 mark: (iii) B, reading antennae present at 2b and one pair of antennae at 3a.
1 mark: (iv) D, reading two pairs of antennae at 3b.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.
objective_titles: Construct and use simple dichotomous keys based on easily identifiable features

items.prompt: Outline the structure of a virus. State how this differs from the structure of a single-celled organism.
items.canonical_answer: Genetic material is enclosed in a protein coat. A virus is non-cellular: it has no cell structure, such as cytoplasm or a cell membrane, whereas a single-celled organism, such as a bacterium, is one complete cell.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: names the genetic material inside the virus.
1 mark: names the protein coat that surrounds it.

1 mark: states the difference, that a virus is non-cellular, with no cell structure, whereas a single-celled organism is one complete cell. Saying only that a virus has no nucleus earns no mark, because bacteria have no nucleus either.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.
objective_titles: Outline the structure of a virus as a protein coat and genetic material

items.prompt: Discuss one argument for and two arguments against classifying viruses as living organisms.
items.canonical_answer: For: a virus carries genetic material, and it reproduces inside host cells. Against: a virus is non-cellular, and it does not respire, feed or grow by itself. Overall, viruses are usually treated as a borderline case.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: gives one argument for: carries genetic material, or reproduces inside host cells.
1 mark: gives one argument against from: non-cellular; does not respire or carry out its own metabolism; does not feed, grow or excrete by itself.

1 mark: gives a second, different argument against from the same list. Needing a host cell to reproduce can be credited on one side only, not as both a for and an against point. No separate mark is given for an overall judgement.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.
objective_titles: Consider the arguments for and against classifying viruses as living organisms

items.prompt: List two leaf or root features typical of monocotyledons.
items.canonical_answer: Parallel leaf veins and a fibrous root system.

1 mark: names a fibrous root system as the second feature.

items.prompt: List two external features useful for identifying a snail as a mollusc.
items.canonical_answer: A soft, unsegmented body and a muscular foot. A shell is also accepted for a snail, although some molluscs, such as slugs, have none.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: names one creditable feature from: a soft, unsegmented body (one point); a muscular foot; a shell, which a snail has although not every mollusc does.
1 mark: names a second, different feature from the same list; the same idea in other words earns no further mark.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.
objective_titles: List the visible external features used to classify molluscs

items.prompt: List two external features of an earthworm useful in classification.
items.canonical_answer: A long body of repeated ring-like segments, and no jointed legs. Small bristles are also accepted.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: names one creditable feature from: a body of repeated ring-like segments; no jointed legs; small bristles.
1 mark: names a second, different feature from the same list; the same idea in other words earns no further mark.

items.prompt: List two diagnostic external features of an adult insect.

marking_guidance: 1 mark: names one creditable feature from: three pairs of jointed legs; a body in three regions; one pair of antennae.
1 mark: names a second, different feature from the same list; the same idea in other words earns no further mark.

items.prompt: Observe a common local invertebrate animal, such as a beetle, an ant, a woodlouse or a snail. Draw a labelled line drawing of it, showing its relative proportions, and label at least two features that show which group it belongs to.
items.canonical_answer: A line drawing with a clear, continuous outline and no shading; the main parts in realistic relative sizes; ruled label lines that end on the structures; at least two labels naming features that show the group. For an ant: three body regions, three pairs of legs on the thorax and one pair of antennae, labelled head, thorax, abdomen, leg and antenna.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the outline is drawn in clear, continuous lines with no shading.
1 mark: the relative sizes of the main parts match this specimen as observed, for example an ant’s abdomen compared with its thorax.
1 mark: label lines are ruled and each one ends on the structure it names.
1 mark: at least two labels name features that place the animal in its group, because these are the diagnostic features, for example three pairs of legs or three body regions for an insect.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.
objective_titles: Observe and draw organisms found locally, concentrating on diagnostic features and/or features that adapt them to their environment

items.prompt: An animal has five pairs of jointed legs and two pairs of antennae. A learner says it must be an arachnid, because it has more legs than an insect. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: An arachnid has exactly four pairs of legs and no antennae, so an animal with antennae cannot be an arachnid. Two pairs of antennae and more than four pairs of legs are crustacean features, so the animal is a crustacean.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: names the mistake: an arachnid has four pairs of legs and no antennae, so the two pairs of antennae rule an arachnid out.
1 mark: states that the animal is instead a crustacean, because two pairs of antennae and more than four pairs of legs are crustacean features.
items.provenance: Original Codex authoring for Biology 6116; marking guidance proposed, not official.
objective_titles: List the visible external features used to classify crustaceans

items.prompt:
1. Which two parts form a binomial name?
A. Family and class
B. Genus and specific name
C. Order and phylum
D. Common name and habitat

2. Which of these groups is the narrowest?
A. Kingdom
B. Family
C. Genus
D. Species

3. Which of these is non-cellular?
A. A virus
B. An insect
C. A fungus cell
D. A mammalian cell

4. What encloses viral genetic material?
A. Cellulose wall
B. A nucleus
C. Protein coat
D. Muscular foot

5. Which feature is typical of monocotyledons?
A. Two cotyledons
B. Network veins
C. Fibrous roots
D. Flower parts mainly in fives

6. Which feature most clearly identifies a bird?
A. Flight
B. Feathers
C. Four limbs
D. Living on land

7. Which arthropod group has no antennae?
A. Typical insect
B. Typical crustacean
C. Typical arachnid
D. Typical myriapod

8. Which is a reliable reptile feature?
A. Dry scales
B. Four legs in every member
C. Feathers
D. Moist scaleless skin

9. An unfamiliar specimen has three leg pairs, one antenna pair and three body regions. Which group fits?
A. Arachnid
B. Annelid
C. Insect
D. Crustacean

10. A plant has network leaf veins and flower parts in fives. Which additional feature is most consistent?
A. One cotyledon
B. Two cotyledons
C. Two antenna pairs
D. Feathers

11. A key first separates jointed legs present from absent. Which choice applies to an earthworm?
A. Present
B. Absent
C. Both
D. Neither because it moves

12. Two organisms share a genus but have different complete species names. What follows?
A. Same species
B. Different kingdoms
C. Different species within the genus
D. No shared family
items.canonical_answer:
1: B. B: a binomial name is the genus followed by the specific name. A and C are levels of the hierarchy, and D is not part of a scientific name.
2: D. D: species is the narrowest level. Kingdom, family and genus each contain more organisms.
3: A. A: a virus is not made of cells. B, C and D are cells or are made of cells.
4: C. C: a protein coat encloses viral genetic material. A and B are parts of cells, and D is a mollusc structure.
5: C. C: monocotyledons have fibrous roots. A, B and D are dicotyledon features.
6: B. B: only birds have feathers. Some birds cannot fly, and four limbs and living on land are shared with other groups.
7: C. C: arachnids have no antennae. Insects and myriapods have one pair and crustaceans two pairs.
8: A. A: every reptile has dry, scaly skin. Snakes have no legs, feathers belong to birds and moist scaleless skin to amphibians.
9: C. C: an insect has all three features. Arachnids have four pairs of legs, annelids have no jointed legs and crustaceans have two pairs of antennae.
10: B. B: network veins and flower parts in fives are dicotyledon features, and dicotyledons have two cotyledons. A is a monocotyledon feature, and C and D are animal features.
11: B. B: an earthworm has no jointed legs. Being able to move says nothing about whether it has legs.
12: C. C: a genus can hold several species. Different specific names mean different species, and organisms in one genus share their kingdom and family.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for each question answered with the correct option (the key), twelve marks in all.
A wrong option (distractor), or more than one option chosen, earns no mark for that question.

items.prompt:
Specimen P has three pairs of legs and one pair of antennae. Specimen Q has five pairs of legs and two pairs of antennae. Suppose a beetle is given the scientific name Genora alba.
(a) Name P’s group. [1]
(b) Name Q’s group. [1]
(c) State which part of Genora alba is the genus and which is the specific name. [2]
(d) Using the descriptions of P and Q, explain why they should not be put in the same arthropod group. [2]
(e) Suggest why a shared brown colour would be weaker classification evidence than the appendage counts. [2]
items.canonical_answer: (a) Insect. (b) Crustacean. (c) Genora is the genus; alba is the specific name. (d) P has three pairs of legs whereas Q has five, and P has one pair of antennae whereas Q has two, so they have different diagnostic features. (e) Colour can vary within a group and can be shared by unrelated animals; leg and antenna counts are structural features that fall in a set range for each group and differ between groups.
marking_guidance: One creditable point earns each mark. (a) 1 mark: insect for P. (b) 1 mark: crustacean for Q.
(c) 1 mark: Genora is the genus.
1 mark: alba is the specific name.
(d) 1 mark: contrasts the leg pairs, three for P and five for Q.
1 mark: contrasts the antenna pairs, one for P and two for Q.
(e) 1 mark: says colour can vary within a group or be shared by unrelated animals.
1 mark: says leg and antenna counts are structural features that fall in a set range for each group and so distinguish groups.

items.prompt:
A learner samples equal 1 m² patches of leaf litter in open and shaded positions, with the same search time of five minutes per patch. The counts of animals with jointed legs are example data.

| Position | Patch 1 / number | Patch 2 / number | Patch 3 / number |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Open | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| Shaded | 8 | 10 | 12 |

(a) Identify the comparison factor and the measured response. [2]
(b) Calculate the mean count in each position. [2]
(c) Describe the comparison supported by these data. [1]
(d) State one other variable, not already given, that should be kept the same in the method. [1]
(e) Some animals hide deep in the litter. Suggest how missing them could bias the comparison between open and shaded patches, and suggest one improvement. [2]
(f) Animal A has three pairs of jointed legs and one pair of antennae. Animal B has seven pairs of jointed legs and two pairs of antennae. Name the arthropod group of each animal. [2]
items.canonical_answer: (a) Position, open or shaded; count of animals found per patch in five minutes. (b) Open mean 4, shaded mean 10. (c) More were found in shaded patches in this sample. (d) Depth of leaf litter, time of day, or the same person searching. (e) If animals hide more easily in one position, for example in thicker litter in the shade, a larger share would be missed there, so the difference between the means would be wrong. Improvement: sift all the litter from each patch thoroughly, for example on a white tray, so hidden animals are found in both positions. (f) A is an insect; B is a crustacean.
marking_guidance: (a) 1 mark for naming position, open or shaded, as the variable being compared.
1 mark for naming the count of animals as the measured response.
(b) 1 mark for each correct mean from the table data: open 4, shaded 10.
(c) 1 mark for the trend that more animals were found in the shade; accept a supporting comparison such as means of 4 and 10.
(d) 1 mark for one other variable kept the same in the method, such as litter depth, time of day or the same searcher.
(e) 1 mark for the limitation that hidden animals may be missed more in one position than the other, which distorts the comparison.
1 mark for an improvement that finds hidden animals, such as sifting all the litter thoroughly.
(f) 1 mark: A is an insect.
1 mark: B is a crustacean.
